source: Julius Obsequens, Liber Prodigiorum (attalus.org English translation)
sample_method: systematic, every 3rd entry from the parsed 81, first 27 taken (no cherry-picking)
annotated_by: manual read of full entry text, 2026-08-15

criteria.date: consular year + editor's B.C. equivalent. Present on 81/81 entries, so date is never the limiting factor for Roman.
criteria.usable: contains at least one celestial event the deterministic engine can actually compute and verify (eclipse, conjunction, moon phase / first visibility, planetary position, identifiable comet)
criteria.ambiguous: contains a genuinely celestial or sky event the engine cannot deterministically produce (meteor, bolide, aurora, parhelion, solar/lunar halo, unidentifiable 'torch' or 'star')
criteria.reject: no celestial content at all: terrestrial, meteorological, biological or political prodigies only

false_positive_trap: Keyword matching on planet names does NOT work for Roman. 'Jupiter', 'Mars', 'Venus' and 'Mercury' in Obsequens almost always denote temples, statues and cult objects, not planets ('The spears of Mars moved' = the statue in the Regia; 'the temple of Jupiter was struck by lightning'). A naive whitelist scan reports 41% celestial content; reading the entries gives roughly 18%. This directly affects the deterministic-whitelist validator in plan.md Section 2.

entries.why: thunderbolt, storm-clouds in clear sky, earth rain, mule birth. Meteorological and terrestrial only.
blood rain, new maritime island, Hannibal's death.
rain, lightning, earth tremor. 'Jupiter' here is the lectisternium, not the planet.
plague, no vulture appeared.
pestilence, doors opening, wolves at midday.
storm damage to the Capitol.
fire at Rome, Regia burnt.
famine, pestilence, hermaphrodite birth.
fire, deformed birth, blood springs, lightning.
Gracchus omens, ravens, milk rivers, owl. No sky event.
snakes portending bloodshed; text also heavily lacunose.
milk rain, lightning-struck flock, two-headed calf.
hermaphrodite, purification rite.
lightning death with an explicit haruspical interpretation. Textbook omen_interpretation structure but the trigger event is meteorological, so the celestial engine cannot condition on it.
firebird, cannibalism, floods, milk rain, deformed twins.

'At the third hour of the day the disappearance of the sun obscured the light' = solar eclipse, computable. Plus 'the moon with a star appeared between the third and the seventh hour', a daytime moon-plus-planet sighting. Haruspical response and expiation both present.
blazing falling torch (bolide) and a shield-like orb crossing the sky at sunset. Genuinely celestial, not deterministically computable.
hermaphrodite, ground roaring, wall collapse, statue turning.
'a new moon waned and did not reappear except on the following day at the third hour' = delayed first visibility of the crescent, exactly the phenomenon class the visibility layer is being built for.
two bolide descriptions, one said to cover the sun. Sky events, not computable.
'the sky seemed to fall down', Pompeius killed by 'the star's fiery breath'. Celestial vocabulary, too vague to pin to an event.
snakes in a bedroom, hawk on the head.
dream of Proserpina, wind, sacrificial bull.
'the entire day previously had been clear, around the eleventh hour night extended itself, then restored the gleam of day' = daytime darkness, solar eclipse, computable and datable.
mule birth interpreted as civil discord, city fire.
entrails without a heart, Calpurnia's dream. The moon appears only as incidental scene-setting, not as the prodigy.

'three suns were seen at around the third hour of the day, then they drew together as one globe' = parhelion, and a nocturnal light bright as daybreak. Sun altitude is computable but ice-crystal optics are not predictable.

full_corpus_check.method: read the matching sentence of every one of the 81 entries flagged by a celestial-vocabulary regex, to confirm the 27-entry sample was not unrepresentative
hard_computable_entries: 20 (147 BC, solar halos + a star blazing 32 days = comet)
68 (44 BC, solar halo + the sidus Iulium comet at the 11th hour)
full_corpus_check.conclusion: the sample rate and the full-corpus rate agree within a few points, so 11% usable is a real number, not a sampling artifact

caveat: This usable rate is measured against the astronomy-conditioned architecture in plan.md Section 2, where the Roman path feeds through the celestial engine. Measured instead as 'has a date + any prodigy + a period-voice interpretation', Obsequens scores very high (essentially 81/81) because every entry is dated by consulship and most carry an expiation or haruspical response. Which number matters depends on whether Roman is required to be astronomically conditioned. Flagged for the 3-vs-5 decision rather than resolved here.
